PointVS was compared to a selection of state-of-the-art pose classification and affinity prediction tools—both machine learning and classical—on the CASF16 docking power and scoring power tests.
Docking power refers to a scoring function’s ability to identify a ligand’s native binding pose among decoys.
It is quantified using Top-N, which is the percentage of systems with a ‘good’ pose ranked in the top N. A pose is considered good if the RMSD to the crystal pose is less than 2Å .
Top-N pose ranking performance on the gninaSetP ose set is shown in Fig 2.3.
When the training sets are the same, PointVS ranks a good pose at the top in 70% of cases, as opposed to 68% with gnina.
When PointVS is trained on the smaller Redocked\gninaSetP ose80 set, such that no similar proteins or ligands as the test set are seen during training, this drops to 68%.
This suggests that for pose prediction, filtering the dataset to remove overlap between train and test structures only causes a minor decrease in docking power.

The Top-1 pose ranking results for the Core set (the CASF16 docking power set) are shown in Table 2.3, for both the case where the crystal pose is included amongst the poses to be ranked, and the case where it is not.

The difference in performance between all of the methods is minimal, and is not affected significantly by whether or not the training data has been filtered for structural similarity (the without-ligand test set scores are 85.3%, 84.9% and 84.2% for PointVS trained on Redocked, Redocked\CoreR and Redocked\Core80 , respectively).

This lack of dependence on debiasing is in agreement with the docking power results shown in Fig 2.3, although the performance of Autodock Vina is comparable with the machine learning methods in this test.
The scoring power is defined by Su et al. as “the ability of a scoring function to produce binding scores in a linear correlation with experimental binding data” (Su et al. 2019).
This is best measured using the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) between the score given by the scoring function and the measured binding affinity data.
For training our networks, we once again used both filtered and unfiltered versions of the PDBBind General dataset to test the influence of dataset bias.
We trained PointVS to classify on Redocked\Core80 , and then switched out the final layer for multi-target regression trained on General\Core80 .

We also used the gnina model trained on the PDBBind General set supplied as part of work by McNutt et al. 2021 to find the PCC on the Core set, but again emphasise that the training data for this model includes many proteins and ligands which are similar or identical to those in the Core set.
This model achieves a PCC of 0.816.
The results from other methods can be seen in Table 2.4.

The three best methods without dataset filtering (gnina, PointVS and ∆VinaXGB) achieve very similar performance, and PointVS outperforms the best non-machine-learning methods from the original CASF16 work (Su et al. 2019), Autodock Vina, significantly (0.805 vs 0.601).

However, the performance of PointVS when trained on the filtered dataset General\Core80 is a better indicator of its true performance on unseen protein-ligand combinations with no analogues in the training data.

To test whether the drop in the performance of PointVS when similar structures are removed from the training set is related to bias or change in training data size, we trained PointVS on General\CoreR .
This has the same training set size as General\Core80 , but can still contain similar structures to those in the test set.
PointVS trained on the General\CoreR achieves a PCC of 0.803 on the CASF16 set.
This is almost identical to the PCC of PointVS trained on the entire General set (PCC of 0.805), and significantly higher than PointVS trained on the General\Core80 set (PCC of 0.754).
This once again points to the performance of these methods when trained and tested using biased datasets being boosted.
This contrasts with our findings in pose prediction performance, in which we saw very minimal change when filtering was performed.
As PointVS trained and tested in a debiased way still appears to be predictive of binding affinity, we next explored whether it had learnt to identify important interactions in the binding site.
PointVS appears to offer a substantial improvement in predictive performance of binding affinity over non-machine-learning methods.
However, MLBSFs are notoriously difficult to interpret.

Good performance when trained on debiased training data is circumstantial evidence that the interatomic interactions involved in binding are being learned, but demonstrating that the attribution scores of PointVS relate to important binding interactions is a more direct measure.
We next present several results demonstrating that important interatomic interactions have been learnt by PointVS.
The protein-ligand interaction profiler (PLIP) (Salentin et al. 2015) uses simple geometric rules to predict interactions at the interface between a protein and a ligand.

We used PLIP to identify the ‘most important’ bonds for three human Tankyrase-2 inhibitors, and examined whether the atoms forming these bonds were highlighted when attribution was carried out on gnina (Koes et al. 2013), IGN (Jiang et al. 2021), and PointVS.
The structures of three tankyrase inhibitors are shown in Fig 2.4.
The top row (structures a, b and c) shows the PLIP analysis of each structure.

The structures in the other three rows show the results of attribution with gnina (second row, structures d, e and f), IGN (third row, structures g, h and i), and PointVS (bottom row, structures j, k and l).

The structures in the second row are coloured by the scores obtained from atom masking with gnina, with atoms contributing negatively to binding being shown in red (negative score), neutral atoms in white, and positively-contributing atoms in green (positive score).

Attribution with IGN and PointVS—which was carried out with bond masking and edge attention analysis, respectively—resulted in scores corresponding to interactions between pairs of atoms rather than individual atoms.

The five highest-scoring edges for structures using both of these methods are shown in the bottom two rows, with dark red lines representing high scores from IGN in structures g, h and i, and darker pink representing higher scores from PointVS in structures j, k and l.
Considering the first column, the two ligand atoms that form hydrogen bonds with the protein as calculated by PLIP (Fig 2.4a) are scored by gnina as the 6th and 8th most important of 20 (Fig 2.4d).
Of the two hydrogen bonding protein atoms, gnina recognises one of them as being extremely important (the highest scoring protein atom), and the other as neutral.

The second structure, Fig 2.4e, shows a similar story, with the three important ligand atoms as given by PLIP (Fig 2.4b) scoring 4th, 7th and 8th out of 20, but the protein atoms they respectively bind to scoring negatively, neutrally and very slightly positively.

In the third structure, the three bound ligand atoms as identified by PLIP (Fig 2.4c) are scored 11th, 13th and 14th of 30 ligand atoms, with the corresponding protein atoms scoring negatively, weakly positively and moderately positively (Fig 2.4f).
Interestingly, the last two structures both contain halogen bonds, and in both cases gnina ranks the ligand atom as important, and the protein atom as a negative contribution.
Overall, gnina struggles to identify important individual atoms (both in the ligand and protein) for binding.

The atoms being scored individually rather than by pairs as with bond masking or edge attention (see below) makes it more difficult to identify the bonds that are being formed: of the bonds identified by PLIP, only in the first structure was there an example where both the protein and ligand atoms were given a high score by gnina, making it the only case where an important bond was identified.

When we performed atom masking on PointVS, we found that the results were similar to those from gnina, in that the atoms contributing to bonds were scored highly but not necessarily enough to recognise their true importance.
However, as described below, we found that edge-based attribution methods provided a clearer insight into important interactions.
The first of the results achieved with edge-based attribution methods is the third row of Fig 2.4, which shows the edges found to be important when carrying out bond masking with IGN.
In the first structure, Fig 2.4g, the bond highlighted as most important connects a ligand atom that PLIP highlights as forming a hydrogen bond (Fig 2.4a) with a different protein atom.

At first glance, it appears that IGN has incorrectly predicted the formation of a hydrogen bond between these atoms, but it should be noted that the atoms that this edge connects are both in aromatic rings that PLIP identifies as being involved in a π-stacking interaction.
IGN also correctly identifies a hydrophobic interaction, which is ranked as the second most important edge.
In the second structure (Fig 2.4h), we again see edges connecting rings involved in π-stacking in Fig 2.4b, this time ranked first and fifth most important.
However, none of the other interactions shown to be taking place in 2.4b—neither the hydrogen nor the halogen bonds—are recognised.

This contrasts the third structure, 2.4i, which shows that IGN has identified the ligand atom that forms a halogen bond as extremely important, with all five of the highest-scoring edges connecting it to various protein atoms.
The edge that connects it to the oxygen atom that PLIP identifies as being the other contributor to this bond (Fig 2.4c) is ranked third most important.
In contrast to the first two structures, little importance is ascribed to the edges connecting the aromatic rings involved in π-stacking.
Altogether, the edges identified as important by performing bond masking with IGN show some agreement with PLIP.
This is especially true of π-stacking interactions, of which it identifies two of three, and the least true of hydrogen bonds, of which it identifies none.

In all three structures, IGN appears to successfully identify one of the interactions taking place (π-stacking in the first two, g and h, and halogen bonding in the third, i) but fails to identify any beyond those.

Considering the first example in the final row of Fig 2.4, we see that the bonds ranked first and second most important by PointVS (Fig 2.4j) correspond to the hydrogen bonds identified by PLIP (Fig 2.4a).
Edges between the two aromatic rings involved in π-stacking are also given high importance scores, being ranked fourth and fifth most important.

We see a similar pattern for the second structure, where the atoms involved in hydrogen bonds as defined by PLIP (Fig 2.4b) are connected by edges assigned high importance by PointVS (ranked first and second most important, Fig 2.4k).
We also again see high scores assigned to the edges connecting the rings involved in π-stacking.
PointVS does, however, fail to recognise the edge joining the atoms involved in the halogen bond shown in green in Fig 2.4b.
In the third example structure, PointVS also identifies the hydrogen bonds identified by PLIP (Fig 2.4c) as being important, again ranking them as the most and second most important edges (Fig 2.4l).
The other edges assigned high importance correspond to hydrophobic interactions.
The results above suggest that of the attribution methods tested, the two edgebased approaches are more effective at identifying important interactions taking place.
However, of the two tested, only edge attention analysis with PointVS was able to reliably identify more than one of the bonds that PLIP identified as forming.
This highlights that edge attention is a useful method for attribution, but further, that PointVS has gone some way to learning to identify important binding interactions.

By performing attribution with edge attention scores on a crystal structure of a given protein with a small molecule bound, binding information in the form of an importance score for every protein atom less than 6Å away from any ligand atom is obtained.
In cases where a fragment screen has been carried out on a target, this attribution process can then be repeated for several crystal structures.
An importance score for each protein atom is then obtained for every bound structure, so we to obtain an average importance score for each of the protein atoms.
This list of protein atoms and associated scores can then be used to inform molecule generation.
To verify that performing attribution with PointVS results in important binding interactions being identified, we perform attribution on the PDBBind Core set (the CASF16 test set).
We compare the bonds highlighted as important for each structure with those highlighted by PLIP.
We then calculated the PCC between the scores assigned to the top five and top ten scoring protein atoms, and the distance between the protein atom and the corresponding ligand atom.
This results in a PCC of -0.766 for the top five protein atoms, and -0.844 for the top ten protein atoms.
This negative correlation implies that protein-ligand atom pairs that are close together (which in turn PLIP is more likely to consider as forming a bond) are commonly identified by PointVS.

We also calculated the correlation coefficient between the ranks of the top five and ten protein atoms and their distance-based rank (this corresponds to the protein atoms ranked by distance to the nearest ligand atom), and obtain 0.719 and 0.788, respectively.
This provides evidence that PointVS is identifying bonds that at the very least make sense geometrically, but not relying on interatomic distances entirely.
We carried out this process for gnina: an alternative CNN-based MLBSF (Koes et al. 2013).
Due to the architecture of gnina, attribution was carried out with masking in place of edge attention analysis.
Masking is a process by which the importance of different atoms can be ascertained.
It is carried out by calculating the difference between the score given when an atom i is removed from the set of input atoms, X, and the score when it is present.
The importance of atom i ∈ X is therefore defined as:
Masking is a significantly more computationally challenging process than edge attention analysis.
To account for this, we used only 20 randomly selected structures from the PDBBind Core set.
We also performed attribution with PointVS on this subset for comparison.
The results of calculating both the PCC and the rank correlation, ρ, are shown in Table 2.5.

On this smaller set we again see a negative correlation between the score assigned by PointVS and the distance between the atoms, and a positive correlation between their rankings by distance and PointVS.
When using gnina, by contrast, we see a much weaker correlation for both of these tests.
This suggests we might be able to use it to identify important bonds—and therefore atoms—involved in binding.

Having shown that PointVS is potentially capable of identifying important binding interactions, we next assessed whether it can be used as a method for extracting structural information from a number of bound structures, and hence used to guide molecule design.

To do this, we extracted hotspot maps from PointVS by performing edge attention attribution on fragment screen data, and compared the resulting hotspots to those found using a data-driven approach, the Hotspots API (Curran et al. 2020).
Our first test used the non-covalent bound structures available for Mpro.
The dataset available for this target is far more extensive than most targets will benefit from, as it is comprised of not only fragment-like molecules, but also follow-up compounds.
These follow-up compounds, which have been curated with the specific intention of targetting important protein atoms, consist of closely related compounds with the same basic scaffold.

Intuitively, the presence of high-quality compounds should result in PointVS being able to extract higher-quality hotspots, as the bound ligands were designed to interact with protein atoms that have been experimentally validated to be important.

We used this dataset as a starting point to verify that, given a selection of bound structures, PointVS can be used to identify these important protein atoms in a way that is useful for fragment elaboration.
The data was extracted from the fragalysis platform (XChem @ Diamond 2024).
A full list detailing the structures used is given in Appendix A.3.
The hotspots identified by the Hotspots API and attribution with PointVS are shown in Fig 2.5a and b.
The hotspots of the two methods will not fall on exactly the same points, as the PointVS hotspots correspond to protein atoms, and the API hotspots to points in the binding pocket.
Still, the two methods clearly highlight very separate regions of the binding pocket as important.
As mentioned previously, the Mpro dataset contains a significant number of closelyrelated follow-up compounds with the same basic scaffold.

To ensure that PointVS is providing a novel insight into important binding regions in the pocket of Mpro and not highlighting important protein atoms by simply counting the number of times they are within close proximity of a ligand donor or acceptor atom, we used PLIP to extract the protein atoms that could be forming hydrogen bonds with ligand atoms for every bound structure.
We then defined any protein atom that was highlighted more than five times across the 152 bound structures as a PLIP hotspot.
This cutoff of five interactions resulted in only four hotspots being extracted.
These top four are shown in Fig 2.5c, and correspond to protein atoms that were highlighted by PLIP 146, 40, 9 and 5 times out of the possible 152.
All but one of the PLIP hotspots are within 2Å of one of the top five PointVS hotspots.

However, the top-ranking PLIP hotspot (which corresponds to a protein atom that forms a hydrogen bond in 146 of the 152 bound structures) is ranked second by PointVS, and the second PLIP hotspot (which PLIP identifies as interacting with ligand atoms in 40 structures) is ranked top by PointVS.

As the first PLIP hotspot is at most the length of one hydrogen bond away from a ligand acceptor in almost every structure, we would expect a geometry-based method to clearly identify it as the top hotspot, as PLIP does.
This is some evidence that PointVS is identifying important protein atoms with a more nuanced approach than simply counting interactions identified with geometric rules.

These results do not mean the PointVS hotspot extraction method is immune to being biased when supplied with fragment screens containing clusters of ligand donor and acceptor atoms, but it is a promising sign that it is not entirely biased by such clusters, and that PointVS is still able to look past them and identify other areas in the pocket as important.

This is a particularly useful finding, given that recent research into fragment screen libraries has highlighted that even screens designed to be diverse structurally still offer a limited exploration of protein pockets (Carbery et al. 2022).

Given that PointVS identifies sites that are different from a traditional hotspot method and a geometry-based method, we next tested whether the high-scoring sites identified by PointVS are dependent on the size of the input fragment set.
To do this, we performed the same hotspot extraction process as before, but instead of using all of the bound structures of Mpro at once, we randomly sampled smaller sets from the collection.
We varied the size of the set sampled between 10 and 80.
This random sampling process was carried out 40 times for each dataset size.
We then performed the hotspot extraction process as before, and took the top five highest-scoring hotspots generated using PointVS with each randomly sampled set of fragment hits.
The results of this are shown in Fig 2.6, where we took samples of size 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80 from the available bound structures.

We see that when the hotspot maps are extracted from a smaller number of bound structures, a wider range of protein atoms are identified as being important; PointVS is less capable of consistently picking out the same five protein atoms every time, and increasing the number of bound structures given to PointVS results in more consistent hotspot maps being generated.

Nevertheless, we note that even when using the smallest datasets containing only 10 bound structures, the five hotspots that are identified when using the full fragment screen are the most commonly included, hence their darker colour in Fig 2.6.
This is a promising sign that attribution with PointVS could still be a useful tool for less well-studied targets.

Having demonstrated that the PointVS hotspots are consistent amongst themselves, and that they highlight different areas in the Mpro active site to the API hotspots, we assessed whether they correctly highlight important areas by performing fragment elaboration.

If PointVS is successfully identifying important interactions, molecules generated to satisfy the pharmacophoric constraints imposed by PointVS hotspots should be as good, if not better, than the molecules using the API hotspots.
For every target tested, the highest scoring elaborations by our ∆SLE20 metric were generated using the top five PointVS hotspots (Table 2.7).
Elaborations made using the hotspots ranked 6-10 by PointVS consistently have worse ∆SLE20 s than those ranked 1-5.

By contrast, the Hotspots API successfully identified ten high- scoring hotspots (indeed, on average, these top ten hotspots produced elaborations with higher standardised ligand efficiencies than the PointVS hotspots), but was unable to successfully rank them amongst themselves.
The accurate ranking of hotspots is important, as in real-world fragment-to-lead campaigns, only a small number of them can easily be targeted.
Within the PointVS hotspot scores, we see that the Mpro hotspots are lower scoring than those for the other two targets.
This can be attributed to the 109 starting fragments for Mpro being of higher quality, having been extracted from curated follow-up compounds rather than fragments.
The improvement that is made on them by elaborating is thus less significant.

This chapter covered the development of PointVS, an EGNN-based method for affinity prediction, and the first ML-based method for extracting important binding information from a target for molecule design.
During the development of PointVS, a commonly used benchmarking protocol for MLBSFs, CASF16, was found to overestimate their accuracy.
In light of this, PointVS was trained and tested on a filtered dataset, and hence encouraged to learn the rules governing intermolecular binding rather than memorise training data.

We showed that when trained on this filtered dataset, PointVS achieves comparable results to other leading scoring functions, providing some evidence that it is successfully identifying important binding interactions.

We provide further proof of this by performing attribution, and showing that PointVS is able to identify important interactions in line with those found by PLIP, a distance-based tool for profiling protein-ligand interactions.
Finally, we investigated how knowledge of important binding regions could be leveraged in other stages of the drug development pipeline; namely fragment elaboration.
We show that when provided with a set of bound structures, performing attribution on such structures yielded hotspot maps describing important protein atoms.
Using these in unison with a fragment elaboration tool, STRIFE, resulted in improved docking scores for the elaborated molecules compared to when hotspots were obtained with a data-based method.

This is further evidence that PointVS is not learning to memorise ligand information but to recognise important interactions, and additionally constitutes the first ML-based method of extracting structural information from a protein target in a way that is useful for fragment elaboration.

More broadly, our work demonstrates that attribution techniques, when applied to debiased models, can be useful for extracting structural information in a way that can be useful in molecule generation.
The success of FBDD depends on access to high-quality structural data and suitable fragment libraries.
In settings where this data cannot be generated (say, due to cost), or where exploring a broader swathe of chemical space is desirable, researchers use de novo design approaches.
These methods aim to generate entirely new molecular structures with desirable properties, offering a complementary path to fragment-based strategies (see chapter 1).

Among the most promising frameworks for de novo design are diffusion models, which have recently emerged as state-ofthe-art generative methods in both chemistry and beyond (Hoogeboom et al. 2022; Ramesh et al. 2021).
The following chapter explores how diffusion-based methods can be used for molecular design, and in particular, how the plausibility of the molecules they generate can be improved.
This section evaluates our proposed quality conditioning method.
First, we the present ablation tests carried out on the GEOMno h dataset to determine the optimal ratio and distortion level for our negative training examples.
Next, using these optimised parameters, we evaluate the performance of a conditional EDM on the QM9, GEOMno h , and ZINC datasets, comparing it directly to the unconditional model.
Finally, we assess the broader applicability of our quality conditioning approach by testing its effectiveness on two different models, GCDM and MolFM.
To identify the optimal proportion of distorted molecules and the required degree of distortion for effective conditional training, we performed ablation studies using the GEOMno h dataset.
This dataset was selected due to its inclusion of drug-like molecule sizes, unlike QM9, whilst being a more computationally tractable set to train than the ZINC dataset.
For these ablation studies, we sampled 100 molecules per model to efficiently screen the effects of varying both distortion magnitudes and the ratio of distorted to non-distorted molecules.

We introduced varying numbers of distorted molecules at different distortion levels (ranging from 0Å , indicating no distortion, to the maximum distortion, Dmax Å ) into the original GEOMno h dataset.
We defined dataset ratios based on the number of distorted and original molecules: for example, a 1:50 ratio indicates one distorted molecule was added for every fifty original molecules.

We evaluated each model’s performance by training conditioned models and sampling 100 molecules, ensuring that the samples were from the low-distortion-factor region of the learned space (formally, enforcing D = 0Å ).

The model trained on a dataset with a ratio of 1:50 distorted molecules and a maximum distortion of 0.25Å exhibited the joint highest RDKit parsability rate of 97%, and the highest PoseBusters pass rate at 81%.
While several models reached 97% RDKit sanitisation rates (namely 1:20, Dmax = 0.5Å and 1:50, Dmax = 0.5Å ), these models exhibited slightly lower PoseBusters pass rates (75% and 78%, respectively).
Increasing or decreasing Dmax further resulted in PoseBusters performance decreasing across all ratios, primarily due to failures in the internal energy test.

This observation suggests that if the training includes molecules that are too distorted, the model does not effectively learn to distinguish between subtly flawed and acceptable molecular structures.
Distorted molecules should therefore still bear some resemblance to realistic conformers, albeit with deliberately infeasible bond lengths and angles.

On the other hand, insufficient distortion compromises the effectiveness of the conditioning classifier, and the models struggle to distinguish between high-quality and low-quality conformations, leading to poor performance in generating desirable molecules.
These results demonstrate the concept of conditioned training on negative data, and give an idea of the extent of distortion and frequency of distorted molecules to add.
We used a ratio of 1:50, and Dmax = 0.25Å for all subsequent tests, but note that any dataset would likely benefit from different exact values of these parameters.
Dmax (Å ) We also examined the quality of molecules generated when sampling from the low-quality region of the learned space (formally, D = Dmax Å ).
The results of this are shown in Appendix B.1.
The molecules sampled using D= Dmax Å are, as expected, worse than both the conditioned models and the baseline model in terms of PoseBusters pass rates, with the highest reaching only 53%.
This poor performance is mainly attributed to failures in the internal energy test.

Having established the parameters for conditional training datasets in terms of quantity of distorted molecules and extent of distortion, we move on to testing this approach with the other datasets, QM9 and ZINC.
Following the results of the ablation tests, we generated conditional versions of each dataset using parameters Dmax = 0.25Å and a distorted:non-distorted molecule ratio of 1:50.
After training conditional models on these modified datasets, we sampled 1,000 molecules from each and evaluated their quality using RDKit and PoseBusters.
The results of this evaluation are presented in Table 3.2.
Our baseline analysis reveals a clear relationship between molecule size and model performance.
The QM9 dataset, comprising molecules smaller than 9 heavy atoms had the highest baseline performance with RDKit and PoseBusters pass rates of 92.2% and 81.1%, respectively.
The non-conditioned EDM model performed exceptionally well with QM9, surpassing all conditional variants across both evaluation metrics.

This superior performance may be attributed to EDM’s specific development for QM9, coupled with the dataset’s smaller molecular size, which appears to enable better discrimination between high-quality and low-quality conformers without requiring examples of the latter.
The GEOMno h dataset also showed strong baseline performance as assessed with RDKit, with generated molecules achieving a pass rate of 84.7%.
However, the more stringent PoseBusters tests presented more of a challenge, with generated molecules presenting a pass rate of 62.2% for PoseBusters.
This can particularly be attributed to the tests concerning bond lengths (65.6% pass rate), bond angles (73.8%), connectivity (74.4%) and internal energy (75.2%).
Conditional training improved these metrics substantially, reaching pass rates of 96.6% (bond lengths), 93.7% (bond angles), 89.4% (connectivity) and 87.7% (internal energy).
Minor improvements were also seen in the steric clash tests (97.8% to 100%).
The baseline model trained on the ZINC subset exhibited markedly lower performance than the other two datasets, with RDKit sanitisation pass rates of 70.6% and PoseBusters pass rates of 40.0%.
The most prevalent failures occurred in bond lengths and atom connectivity, with pass rates of only 65.0% and 62.4%, respectively.
This performance decline relative to GEOMno h may be attributed to two factors.

Firstly, the ZINC dataset’s increased diversity, featuring unique conformers rather than multiple conformers per molecule (as found in GEOMno h ), may cause the model to prioritise learning atom types over optimising 3D conformer generation.
Secondly, and perhaps more significantly, the compositional differences between datasets may play a crucial role.
While the ZINC subset exclusively contains medium-sized compounds, GEOMno h incorporates the entire QM9 dataset, resulting in a smaller average molecule size.
Conditional training on the ZINC dataset yielded improved RDKit sanitisation rates and PoseBusters scores.

The most notable improvement was observed in the ZINC model’s atom connectivity pass rate, which increased from 62.4% to 95.7%, but improvements were also seen in the pass rates of the tests assessing bond lengths (65.0% to 94.1%), bond angles (75.3% to 93.7%), internal steric clash (79.5% to 99.0%), and internal energy (78.5% to 89.4%).
These results indicate that the baseline EDM’s performance degrades when generating larger molecules, often yielding implausible structures.
Our conditioning method at least partially helps mitigate this decline, increasing the output proportion of high-quality molecules.
We next investigate the use of a more scientifically grounded labelling of the molecules—specifically, using internal energy approximations—for this conditioning process.
The XTB program (Bannwarth et al. 2021) is a computational chemistry software package used for molecular modelling and simulations.
It is based on the semiempirical tight-binding approach, which approximates the electronic structure of molecules using a simplified set of parameters derived from quantum mechanics.
XTB extends traditional tight-binding methods by incorporating additional empirical corrections to improve the accuracy of calculated properties.
It is well-suited for studying large molecular systems where the computational cost of more accurate methods such as density functional theory (DFT) becomes prohibitive.
We use the default implementation of XTB (GFN2-xTB) to perform singlepoint energy calculations for each of the molecules, both distorted and original, for QM9, GEOMno h , and our ZINC dataset.
For the original GEOM dataset, the original conformers have energy annotations calculated with the same method, so we only carry out this calculation for the distorted molecules.

We carry out this process using two different annotation types: a ‘distortion factor’, a quantity that represents the extent to which the coordinates have been altered, and an internal energy value, obtained by scoring both original and distorted conformers with the extended tight binding program (XTB) (Bannwarth et al. 2021).
We’ve observed that for medium-sized, drug-like compounds, conditioning on a distance-based distortion factor results in improvements for RDKit sanitisation and PoseBusters tests.

To investigate whether using a potentially more meaningful label (specifically, an internal energy value obtained using XTB) improves the conditioned models, we used the datasets generated with the previous distortion process.
The distorted molecules were then passed through an XTB single-point energy calculation.
The same calculation was applied to all high-quality, non- distorted molecules in all datasets, excluding the original GEOM dataset, which already has energy annotations calculated with XTB.

We then trained each of the models conditionally, and once trained, we sampled 100 molecules from each, this time enforcing D = Emin , where Emin is a fixed value for each dataset corresponding to the lowest internal energy annotation of any molecule in it.
Then we once again assessed all 100 molecules using RDKit and PoseBusters (Table 3.3).
As observed when conditioning on distortion factor, the model trained on QM9 generated lower quality molecules when conditioning with internal energy was carried out.
Conversely, conditionally training EDM on GEOMno h with internal energy resulted in increased performance compared to both the baseline and the conditioned model using the distance distortion factor.
The RDKit and PoseBusters pass rates reached 98% and 84%, respectively.
The model trained on ZINC, however, exhibited a decrease in both RDKit and PoseBusters pass rate.
These pass rates were also lower than those of the molecules generated with the ZINC model trained conditionally on distortion factor.
When using the distance-based distortion factor, we enforced D=0Å when sampling, as this represented molecules that had not undergone any distortion.
The distortion factor, ranging from 0Å to Dmax Å , provides a straightforward measure of how much the structure of a molecule has been altered.
In contrast, internal energy values, although physically meaningful, are challenging to compare directly between different molecules.

Each molecule can have a low internal energy corresponding to a high-quality conformer and a high one corresponding to a low-quality conformer, but the lowest energy conformers of some molecules may still have higher energy values than the highest energy annotations of others.
This inconsistency likely contributed to the observed performance decreases when conditioning on internal energy.

In this work, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of including low-quality conformers in a training set and conditioning a diffusion model on a label representing conformer quality to enhance the generation of high-quality druglike molecules.
By leveraging datasets derived from GEOM and ZINC, alongside a conditioning method proposed by Hoogeboom et al., we have successfully improved the validity of generated molecules.

Our approach, which focuses on sampling molecules with labels corresponding to low distortion factors, leads to enhancements in RDKit parsability and validity as assessed by PoseBusters for the original EDM, as well as for a subsequent diffusion model, GCDM.

We also explored conditioning on internal energy calculated with XTB as an alternative to the distortion factor, but found that the distance-based distortion metric proved more effective, likely due to challenges in comparing absolute energy values across diverse molecular structures.
The method shows strongest improvements for diffusion-based models, particularly those built on the EDM framework, which comprise a significant portion of current 3D molecule generation approaches.

Testing on MolFM, a flow-matching architecture, yielded inconsistent results across datasets, suggesting that the conditioning approach may interact differently with non-diffusion-based generative models.
The approach is most effective for datasets containing larger, drug-like molecules, as demonstrated by our results with GEOMno h and ZINC.

This can be explained mechanistically; larger molecules have more complex conformational spaces where explicit examples of invalid states help define the boundary between high-quality and low-quality conformers.
Conversely, the method provides limited benefits for datasets like QM9 where molecules are small (fewer than 9 heavy atoms) and have constrained conformational spaces.
In these cases, it appears models can effectively learn to distinguish valid from invalid conformations from the training data alone.
Our findings underscore the importance of considering the quality of conformers in molecule generation processes.

The results show that by training models to discern between favourable and unfavourable molecular conformations, we can selectively sample from the high-quality region of learned space, resulting in significant improvements in the validity of generated molecules.

Moving forward, further research could explore why quality conditioning is effective for certain architectures but not others, and investigate alternative labelling schemes that might generalise across different generative modelling approaches.
Additionally, investigating the applicability of our approach to other areas of molecular design and exploration could yield valuable insights for drug discovery and beyond.
Overall, our study provides a promising avenue for generating valid drug-sized molecules efficiently and effectively using diffusion-based architectures.
Having established the effectiveness of this strategy, we next explore a complementary approach that addresses the same challenge from a different angle.

The following chapter covers a fragment-based method that aims to enforce validity not by refining the training data, but by directly constructing molecules from pre-validated chemical building blocks during the generation process itself.

Initial experiments were conducted using only the basic BRICS decomposition method, as preliminary results quickly highlighted significant issues arising from the lack of rotational information (see Figure 4.4).
To isolate and quantify this problem, we performed a control experiment to establish the theoretical upper bound on reconstruction accuracy for a centroid-only approach.

For this, we took a subset of 100 molecules from our pre-processed GEOM dataset and fed their ground-truth BRICS fragments and centroid coordinates directly into our reconstruction pipeline, bypassing the generative model entirely.
Even with this idealised input, only 48 of the 100 molecules passed RDKit sanitisation checks.

This 48% success rate reveals a fundamental limitation of the representation itself; even with perfect block placement, the ambiguity in fragment orientation leads to chemically invalid structures more than half the time.
This finding provides critical context for the much lower RDKit sanitisation pass rate of approximately 4% observed for molecules generated by the full diffusion model.
This lower rate is a product of two compounding factors: the model’s own errors in learning the placement task, and the inherent flaws of the centroid-only representation.
To address this primary limitation, it became clear that explicitly incorporating rotational information was an essential next step.
As an initial attempt to address the rotational ambiguity observed in the centroidonly approach, we tested a simple geometric post-processing step.
Rather than encoding orientation as additional model inputs, this method attempted to standardise fragment orientations during reconstruction.
For each generated fragment, we computed its best-fit plane using the same procedure described above.
This plane was then aligned to a global plane—found by fitting a plane to the sampled centroids—using a rigid rotation.
The fragment was then translated to place its centroid at the model’s predicted coordinates.
This approach aimed to remove rotational degrees of freedom entirely by imposing a standard orientation on all fragments.

However, as shown in Table 1, this method achieved only a 10.8% RDKit sanitisation pass rate; an improvement over the 4% of the unaligned centroid-only model, but still substantially worse than the atomic model.
Visual inspection revealed that the primary failure mode was incorrect connectivity between fragments.
While individual fragments were now consistently oriented, the fixed canonical orientation was often geometrically incompatible with the correct bonding geometry required to connect adjacent blocks.

This result demonstrated that fragment orientation cannot be handled through post-processing alone; the orientation must be learned and predicted by the model as part of the generative process, motivating the development of the full rotation-aware representation tested next.

Following the analysis of the centroid-only models, we incorporated the position and orientation vectors into two existing frameworks: the full BRICS decomposition and the reduced-library BRICS method.
To directly measure the impact of this new representation, we first repeated the reconstruction control experiment described previously.

Using the ground-truth coordinates and the new orientation vectors for 100 molecules from the full BRICS dataset, our reconstruction pipeline successfully produced 89 molecules that passed RDKit sanitisation checks.

This represents a dramatic improvement from the 48% success rate of the centroid-only approach and confirms that our orientation descriptor, while imperfect, provides substantial and valuable information for molecular reconstruction.
Next, we assessed the performance of the full generative models.
For each of the two methods, 1000 molecules were sampled and subjected to the same RDKit sanitisation check.
The model using the full BRICS library achieved a pass rate of 27.2%.
The model trained on the more constrained, reduced-library BRICS dataset performed significantly better, achieving a pass rate of 51.7%.

While the inclusion of rotational information yielded a marked improvement over the centroid-only models, these results still fall well short of the 84.7% pass rate achieved by the fully atomistic model.
The large gap suggests that the primary challenge lies not just in the model’s ability to place fragments, but in the inherent inconsistency of the fragments themselves.

The geometric diversity of the substructures produced by BRICS decomposition appears too great to allow for the definition of a consistent and reliable local coordinate system using simple geometric heuristics.
This work investigated the adaptation of a successful atomistic diffusion model to a block-based framework for molecular generation.
Our exploration revealed that the choice of fragment representation is a critical determinant of model performance.
Initial models using a simple centroid-only representation were fundamentally capped, unable to exceed a theoretical reconstruction accuracy of 48% due to rotational ambiguity.

The introduction of an explicit 9-dimensional orientation vector helped somewhat alleviate this issue, improving reconstruction fidelity and boosting the final model’s RDKit sanitisation pass rate to a peak of 51.7% with a reduced BRICS fragment library.
Despite these advances, the block-based models did not approach the 85% pass rate of the original atomistic framework.
Our analysis indicates that the primary bottleneck is the high geometric variance within the chemically-derived BRICS fragments.
This diversity prevents simple geometric heuristics from defining a consistent and reliable local coordinate system, which is essential for accurate placement and reconstruction by the model.
The challenges encountered in this work are reflective of the broader difficulties in fragment-based generation, and the successes of subsequent models offer a clear path forward.

The consistent theme among effective hierarchical models like HierDiff is the use of a dedicated decoder module—typically an equivariant neural network— tasked specifically with translating the coarse-grained representation into a valid atomistic structure.
This learned, end-to-end approach to assembly and orientation proves more robust than the predefined geometric heuristics we employed.
Therefore, future research in this area should prioritise the development of these hierarchical architectures.

Combining a simplified and standardised fragment vocabulary, as explored in our own work, with an equivariant decoder represents a promising direction for realising the full potential of block-based molecular generation.

subsection: 5.4.1.1 Direct conditioning with a constant scaling factor
text: This presents a clear trade-off: the directional guidance from the gradient is beneficial, but its magnitude must be carefully controlled to avoid overpowering the model’s learned structural constraints.
To better balance the external conditioning force with the model’s internal potentials, we introduced three scheduling strategies as detailed in section 5.3.1.5: block, global, and block and global.
The objective was to apply a strong conditioning force in early recycling iterations and then allow the model’s learned geometry to regularise the structure in later cycles.
For these experiments, we observed that the coordinate representation could tolerate an increased scaling constant of 1.0 (up from 0.1) when paired with a scheduler.

This increased tolerance is likely attributable to the scheduler, which attenuates the update strength over successive recycling iterations, mitigating the disruptive effect of the large initial scaling factor.
Attempts to apply this increased scaling to the frame and single representations resulted in unstable, disordered predictions, so their scaling constants were maintained at 0.1.
The results, summarised in Fig. 5.4, demonstrate that schedulers did not yield a performance breakthrough, with outcomes largely mirroring those of the constant scaling approach.
The 8FEI target again showed the most consistent improvement, while the method proved detrimental for 8CXO across all configurations.

No single combination of representation and scheduler emerged as a superior strategy, though there were some that were better than others: for instance, the single rep, 0.1, 1, block method was among the worst performers, only improving predictions for half of the targets, whereas the coords, 1.0, 1, global scheme improved results most consistently, lowering RMSDs for 8/10 of the targets.

The lack of a clear best strategy and the limited gains across all methods suggests we had not yet found an optimal strategy for balancing our two objectives: on the one hand, the effective incorporation of experimental data, and on the other, the generation of structurally sound models by OpenFold.
We therefore proceeded to test a different approach by applying a series of smaller, more frequent updates within each structure module block.
To test our hypothesis that multiple, smaller updates to predictions might be less disruptive to the OpenFold inference process, we first implemented a fixediteration scheme.
In this approach, the cycle of map simulation, overlap calculation, gradient computation, and representation update was repeated three times within each structure module block.
This method yielded mixed results (Figure 5.5).

While some targets, such as 7VLR, showed consistent minor improvements (a reduction in RMSD of approximately 1 Å on average), the issue of local minima trapping persisted for others (e.g., 8CXO and 7VPL).
This suggests that iterative updates alone cannot overcome poor initialisation without an element of stochasticity.
To address the potential instability of the fixed-iteration approach, we implemented an adaptive strategy.
Here, the gradient was applied incrementally, and the process was repeated within a cycle only as long as it improved the mapmodel overlap score.
A maximum of 40 iterations was set as a safeguard, though convergence was typically achieved in 15–25 iterations.
The results, presented in Figure 5.6, demonstrate that this adaptive method is more robust.
It produced improvements, reducing the RMSD for 6LN8 from 5.25Å to 4.62Å and for 8FEI from 3.58Å to 2.20Å.

However, this adaptive approach also produced worse failures on certain targets, likely because the large number of cumulative updates, even when applied gradually, can still introduce structural distortions.
Overall, no single conditioning strategy emerged as universally superior across all targets.
The frames, 0.1, 3, block and global scheme was the most consistently positive performer, improving the RMSD for 9 of the 10 targets.

Two of the convergence tracking methods (frames, 0.1, 40, block and global and frames, 0.1, 40, block) and the simpler coords, 1.0, 1, global method also performed well, improving 8 out of 10 targets.
When considering only the targets that saw improvement, the frames, 0.1, 1, block method yielded the highest average improvement of 13.5%.
However, all improvements were marginal.

This highlights a fundamental challenge: the difficulty of inducing large-scale conformational changes without either getting trapped in local minima or destabilising the model’s learned structural priors.
Given the limited success of our OpenFold conditioning experiments we tested an alternative modelling paradigm.

The development of Boltz-2 offered an opportunity to address some of the limitations we had encountered: in particular, as a generative diffusion model, Boltz-2’s prediction process is inherently more suited to external perturbation.
There is strong precedent for guiding, or “drifting”, such models during inference (Ziv et al. 2024).
This suggested that we could apply a more forceful conditioning force to drive conformations towards the experimental data without the structural collapse observed previously.
An additional advantage is Boltz-2’s ability to model protein-ligand interactions, creating a theoretical pathway to apply our method to cryo-EM maps of bound complexes.
We first applied a direct gradient-based optimisation conditioning scheme, analogous to the one we used in our OpenFold method, within the Boltz-2 structure module.
A key advantage of this diffusion-based model is its greater tolerance to external perturbations during the generative process.
Unlike OpenFold, the iterative denoising steps could accommodate an external update without structural collapse.
The results of this approach, summarised in Fig 5.7, show a mixed pattern of success.
While conditioning led to modest improvements over vanilla Boltz-2 for several targets (e.g., 5YW7, 6LN8, and 7N70), it was detrimental to others (e.g., 6LLY and 7VLR).
However, this method proved capable of inducing substantial rearrangements that were unachievable with OpenFold.
This is best exemplified by 8CXO, where the RMSD was reduced from 11.7Å to 7.7Å, and most strikingly for 8FEI, which improved from a baseline of 20.0Å down to 2.4Å.
While these specific successes demonstrate a much higher potential for refinement, the overall inconsistency suggested that this simple implementation was not yet a reliable strategy.

The inconsistency of the direct gradient-based optimisation approach (both in OpenFold and Boltz-2) suggested that intervening late in the process—during structure refinement—was insufficient for inducing large-scale changes.
This led us to explore interventions at an earlier stage of the pipeline.

We took inspiration from two recent works: the ROCKET method of Fadini et al. 2025, which demonstrated the potential of MSA subsampling to explore new conformations, and the CryoBoltz method of Raghu et al. 2025.
Ablation studies from the latter demonstrated that their global conditioning, applied early in the process, had a more substantial impact than their late-stage structure module conditioning.
Based on these insights, we implemented an MSA subsampling procedure.
By providing the model with varied and more sparse subsets of the full MSA, we introduce stochasticity into the prediction process.
The goal is to generate a diverse ensemble of initial structures, effectively allowing the model to explore a broader conformational landscape than is possible from a single, deterministic run.

We hypothesise that this exploration should increase the likelihood of sampling a conformation closer to the experimental structure, which can then serve as a more effective starting point for refinement.
Only MSA subsampling To first isolate the effect of this stochastic sampling, we generated predictions using subsampled MSAs without any gradient-based conditioning.
The results (Fig. 5.8) show that running Boltz-2 with several distinct starting MSAs allows local minima to be escaped more easily.
This is shown in the cases of 7VLR and 7VPL, which saw improvements with this method even though the standard gradient-based optimisation approach alone made them worse.
However, the method is not consistent, as there are still targets for which subsampling makes the models worse.
There is a chance this could be improved by increasing the number of MSAs we start with, but as this is a computationally expensive process, we tested a maximum of five.

Further, there is no clear trend regarding which number of sequences yields the best performance: intuitively, including more sequences should make predictions better by providing a more well-informed starting point, but the higher the number of sequences, the less diverse the different MSAs will be.
This results in less distinct starting points and therefore fewer opportunities for one to align closely with the map.
Given that this approach seemed promising, we next combined it with the gradient-based optimisation method.
Combining with gradient-based optimisation Finally, we combine the MSA subsampling with the conditioning approach, with the results shown in Fig. 5.9.

As with all other methods tested, this approach had varied success, with the best method for each target improving the RMSDs of 5YW7, 6LN8, 7O3D, 7RAV, 7VLR and 7VPL compared to the gradient optimisation or MSA subsampling methods alone.
However, the average RMSD across all targets increased compared to the MSA-subsampling only method, mostly due to a large decrease in quality of the predictions for target 8FEI.

However, as we showed in Fig 5.3, predictions for this target have a tendency to get trapped in a local minima of nearby incorrect density, explaining why the gradient optimisation approach worsens predictions.
It is possible that injecting more stochasticity (say, by subsampling more MSAs) could improve the guidance for this case.
Still, excluding 8FEI, this combination proved to be the most effective approach tested in this chapter.
It is still inconsistent, though, and difficult to identify an optimal MSA number, as the performance with different sequence numbers was much better on some targets than others.
For example, using 2048 sequences resulted in the most reliable improvements overall, but still only had the lowest RMSD for 6/10 targets.

Future directions should accordingly include taking smaller MSA subsamples, as well as carrying out repeat runs to see whether this finding stays consistent, or whether it too is stochastic in nature.
In this work, we explored several strategies for conditioning de novo protein structure prediction models with cryo-EM density maps.

Our initial experiments, which applied a gradient-based force within the structure module of OpenFold, highlighted a fundamental limitation: late-stage interventions struggle to induce large-scale conformational changes without compromising the model’s learned structural priors, leading to disordered or non-physical outputs.
Pivoting to Boltz-2, a diffusion-based model, proved to be a more promising direction.

While a simple gradient-based optimisation approach still yielded inconsistent results, it demonstrated a far greater capacity for making large structural rearrangements, as evidenced by the dramatic improvements for challenging targets such as 8FEI and 8CXO.

Furthermore, our exploration of MSA subsampling confirmed that introducing stochasticity at an early stage is an effective means of broadening the explored conformational landscape and discovering more accurate starting points for refinement.

Future work should investigate the combination of MSA subsampling and gradient-based refinement more systematically, as this approach showed promise but may still be insufficient to escape deep local minima for some targets.
Increasing the number of subsamples or incorporating additional stochastic perturbations—such as random noise injection—could further improve sampling diversity and convergence.

It will also be essential to evaluate performance across a wider range of targets and to perform multiple runs per target, given the variability observed in current predictions (particularly the large disparity among 8FEI predictions in Figure 5.9).
Finally, the present work still relies on RMSD-based alignment to ground-truth structures and on simulated density maps, which are considerably less noisy than experimental data.
Removing these dependencies and extending the approach to real, heterogeneous cryo-EM maps will be crucial steps toward establishing practical, robust conditioning methods.

Nevertheless, the results presented here indicate a promising avenue: early stochastic conditioning combined with physically informed gradient guidance can meaningfully steer diffusion-based models toward conformations consistent with experimental data.

This thesis has presented contributions across multiple aspects of molecular modelling and drug design, spanning virtual screening, generative design (both fragment-based and de novo), and protein structure refinement.
While the approaches differ in scope and methodology, they share a central motivation: to improve the reliability of machine learning applications within the early stages of drug discovery.
In this chapter, we provide concluding remarks for each application and highlight potential directions for future work.
In chapter 2, we introduced an EGNN-based scoring function that we designed to be as unreliant as possible on dataset biases.

By training and testing on a filtered dataset, we showed that the model was less dependent on memorisation than other leading methods, and instead had started to capture aspects of the real physics of protein–ligand binding.

Through interpretability experiments, we also found that the model based its predictions on realistic protein–ligand interactions, and that these signals could be used to guide fragment elaboration in ways that improved docking outcomes.
From this work, two main points stand out.

First, interpretability is not just useful, but should be essential for virtual screening models: without it, there is no clear way to tell if a model is using real binding information or dataset patterns.

Although it would be difficult to implement a single standardised interpretability benchmark that works across all models, it would be valuable if new VS methods were expected to demonstrate their performance on a set of such metrics.
This could help reduce the flood of publications that report high scores on biased datasets, and help to ensure that reported improvements reflect genuine advances.
Second, interpretability methods offer more than just model validation; they can provide structural insights to guide molecule design.
A properly debiased model can screen numerous compounds, identify key recurring interactions, and help prioritise new designs that add or preserve these features.
Still, this work also highlights a key issue.
With the datasets currently available, it is impossible to train scoring functions that are entirely free from bias.
Progress will depend on building large, high-quality public datasets of protein–ligand complexes that are modelled in a consistent way.
Such resources would not only support more reliable benchmarking, but also give ML models a better chance to learn binding physics in a way that generalises beyond narrow training sets.
Our first piece of work on diffusion models for molecule generation (chapter 3) demonstrated the benefits of incorporating negative data by conditioning on conformer quality.

By explicitly including synthetically distorted conformers in the training data and conditioning on so-called distortion labels, we improved the validity and plausibility of generated molecules, particularly for larger, drug-like compounds with complex conformational landscapes.
We next investigated a substructure-based generative model, adapting atomistic diffusion approaches to a block-based setting (chapter 4).

While this direction offers the promise of improved chemical validity through assembly from pre-validated fragments, our results underscore the challenges posed by geometric variance in fragment libraries.

The limitations of orientation schemes point to the need for either learned equivariant decoders capable of reconstructing atomistic detail from coarse-grained representations, or hierarchical approaches that get the generation most of the way toward being a molecule with block based approaches, and then refine the atomistic model.
Two primary takeaways can be drawn from this work.

First, it serves as a reminder that negative data is a valuable tool for improving the performance of machine learning models, even in domains like unconditional molecule generation where training data may seem abundant.
The second, broader takeaway is the importance of mastering foundational principles before applying new, computationally expensive architectures to more complex challenges.
Many current applications of diffusion models for small-molecule generation rely heavily on posthoc filtering to achieve viable results.

This raises the question of whether such resource-intensive architectures are justified if they require extensive filtering, or whether efforts should be redirected toward refining these methods or revisiting more established approaches.
Finally, we explored conditioning protein structure prediction with cryo-EM density maps.
Gradient-based interventions in OpenFold revealed the difficulty of enforcing large-scale conformational changes at late stages without destabilising learned priors.
By contrast, Boltz-2 showed greater capacity for structural rearrangements, particularly when combined with stochasticity via MSA subsampling.
While the results were mixed, these early experiments point towards promising avenues for integrating experimental restraints into generative structure prediction.
This work has laid important groundwork, perhaps more by clarifying which strategies are ineffective than by arriving at a viable one.

Nonetheless, clear next steps have emerged, including sampling more MSAs, experimenting with different conditioning schedulers, and potentially modifying the structure prediction models themselves through fine-tuning to better incorporate experimental data during training.
Such advances would bring generative structure prediction closer to practical utility in cryo-EM model building.
Taken together, the work in this thesis illustrates both the promise and the persistent challenges of applying machine learning to drug discovery and structural biology.
While none of the methods presented constitute a complete solution, each provides new insights into how data quality, model architecture, and conditioning strategies shape outcomes.
Several key lessons stand out: interpretability is central to ensuring that models learn physics rather than artefacts.
Negative data remains a powerful tool for enhancing the robustness of generative models.
Block-based generation is an attractive paradigm but requires sophisticated encoding schemes to overcome the geometric inconsistency of substructures.

Finally, guiding AlphaFold-like predictions towards experimental constraints is feasible but requires intervention early in the generative process, coupled with sufficient stochasticity to escape local energy minima.

Pursuing these directions will require better datasets, more carefully designed benchmarks, and a stronger collective emphasis on interrogating our models rather than relying solely on benchmark scores.

If these challenges can be met, the reward is substantial: machine learning methods that are not only powerful in silico but also robust, interpretable, and truly impactful in real-world biomedical discovery.
